# Problem 1: Cherry Blossoms and Temperature
### Problem 1.1

![March Temperature Anomalies and Cherry Blossom Bloom Date]("figs/11.png"){#fig-11 width=4.5in}

The linear fit suggests that increasing temprature anomalies lead to a decrease in the date of year that the cherry blossom bloom peaks; that is, the bloom occurs earlier in the year. The slope of fit is about -7.8, which suggests that a 1 degree C increase in temperature anomaly leads to a bloom more than one week earlier. 

### Problem 1.2

The mean-squared error for this fitted model on the in-sample data is about 22.32. I was unfortunately having trouble implementing the log-loss in my code; I will attempt to understand how to implement this after the solutions are released.

### Problem 1.3

Using 5-fold cross-validation, the mean-squred errors for each fold were roughly similar to the in-sample data, with MSE values from my run of 34.68, 23.15, 20.46, 22.82, and 18.74. Some of the folds have a lower/better MSE than the full dataset, and some have a higher/worse MSE, but there are no major differences.

```{=latex}
\newpage
```
### Problem 1.4

This model is relatively generalizable. The 5-fold cross-validation did not produce meaningfully worse MSE values than the in-sample model, suggesting that the model was not learning much more information from the full dataset that it could not learn from a much smaller subset. Thus, this model should be similarly good at predicting unseen values as it is at predicting in-sample values.

# Problem 2: Back in Chicago
### Problem 2.1

![Chicago Deaths vs. Time with Linear Fit]("figs/21.png"){#fig-21 width=4.5in}

The linear regression coefficient for this fit is -1.76e-17, very close to zero, and the intercept is 128.75. As visible in @fig-21, there is basically no change in the model predicted number of deaths through time, predicting about 129 deaths throughout the time period. 

```{=latex}
\newpage
```
### Problem 2.2

![Chicago Deaths vs. Temperature with Linear Fit]("figs/22.png"){#fig-22 width=4.5in}

The linear regression coefficient for this fit is -0.29, and the intercept is 129.96. Unlike the time fit, there is a trend in @fig-22, with the coefficient suggesting that the model predicts a decrease of a bit less than 1 death per 3 degrees increase in mean daily temperature. The scatterplot of data appears to follow this decreasing trend; however, the model grossly underestimates the very high deaths during the heat wave.

```{=latex}
\newpage
```
### Problem 2.3

![Chicago Deaths vs. Temperature with Linear Fit incorporating PM25]("figs/23.png"){#fig-23 width=4.5in}

The linear regression coefficients for this fit are -0.37 and 0.215, and the intercept is 129.29. When incorporating the median pm25 concentration, the model predicts a greater decrease in temperature for a given decrease in . However, it also predicts an increase in deaths with increasing pm25 concentration. The resulting slope in @fig-23 is thus very similar to the one in @fig-22. 

```{=latex}
\newpage
```
### Problem 2.4

For the model with temperature only, the 5-fold cross-validation MSE scores are 164.43, 170.09, 178.88, 321.36, and 203.51. For the model with both temperature and pm25 concentration, the MSE scores are 140.53, 170.13, 183.30, 150.67, and 122.85. The dataset has the previously mentioned spike in deaths during the heat wave of 1995; random selection should split up this data, but it may explain the anomalously high MSE values for folds 4 and 5 of the temperature-only dataset if the heat wave days ended up exclusively in that fold. The model with both temperature and pm25 appears to perform better, with lower MSE scores, although not by much.
